meta.name: Bearded Collie
meta.excerpt: The Bearded Collie is a lively, intelligent Scottish herding dog known for its long flowing double coat and boundless enthusiasm. Affectionately called the 'Beardie,' this breed thrives on activity and human companionship.
meta.meta_description: Learn about the Bearded Collie: temperament, grooming needs, health, and whether this energetic Scottish herding breed is right for your family.

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: The Bearded Collie: Scotland's Bouncy Herder
intro.html:
The Bearded Collie, affectionately known as the 'Beardie,' is one of Scotland's oldest herding breeds, developed to work the rugged Highland terrain in all weather conditions. With its distinctive long, flowing double coat and expressive eyes peeking through a curtain of hair, the Beardie is as striking in appearance as it is in personality.

Originally bred to herd sheep and cattle independently across Scotland's challenging landscape, the Bearded Collie developed a keen intelligence and a strong will. These dogs had to make quick decisions without constant handler input, which explains why they can sometimes appear stubborn today. However, their intelligence also makes them capable learners when properly motivated.

The Beardie's personality is often described as 'bouncy' — they greet the world with infectious enthusiasm and rarely slow down. They are deeply affectionate with their families and crave companionship, making them poorly suited to long hours alone. This is a dog that genuinely wants to be part of every aspect of family life, from morning walks to lazy evenings on the couch.

While they have found a popular niche as show dogs and companions, Beardies still carry the heart of a working dog. They excel in dog sports like agility, obedience, and herding trials, and they need significant daily exercise to stay mentally and physically balanced. A bored Beardie is a creative Beardie — and not always in ways their owners appreciate.

appearance.label: Appearance
appearance.heading: Coat, Size, and Distinctive Features
appearance.html:
The Bearded Collie is a medium-sized, athletic dog with a sturdy build that belies its agility. Males typically stand 21–22 inches at the shoulder, while females measure 20–21 inches. Weight ranges from 45 to 55 pounds, with most dogs landing solidly in the middle of that range.

The breed's most defining feature is its magnificent double coat. The outer coat is flat, harsh, and strong — designed to shed rain and dirt. The undercoat is soft, furry, and close. Together they provide excellent weather protection and give the Beardie its characteristic shaggy appearance. The coat falls naturally to either side of the body, and the hair on the face creates the signature 'beard' from which the breed takes its name.

Beardies come in several colors: slate gray, reddish fawn, black, and blue, all with or without white markings in classic collie pattern. Interestingly, Beardie puppies are often born dark and lighten significantly as they mature — a black puppy may become slate gray, and a brown puppy may become fawn. The adult color is not fully established until around 18 months to 3 years of age.

The expression of a Beardie is alert, bright, and inquiring. The eyes are large, soft, and affectionate, harmonizing in color with the coat. Ears are medium-sized, covered with long hair, and hang flat against the head. The tail is set low, carried low when relaxed and raised in a gentle curve when excited — never curled over the back.

temperament.label: Temperament
temperament.heading: Lively, Loving, and a Little Headstrong
temperament.html:
The Bearded Collie temperament is one of the breed's greatest assets and its greatest challenges. These dogs are exuberant, joyful, and deeply loving — but they are also independent thinkers who learned to solve problems on their own while working the Scottish hills. That independence can translate into selective listening if training isn't consistent and engaging.

Beardies are extraordinary family dogs for active households. They adore children and tend to be gentle and playful with them, though their bouncy energy can accidentally knock over very young toddlers. They generally get along well with other dogs and can coexist peacefully with cats, especially when raised together from puppyhood. Their herding instinct may occasionally show up as an urge to round up children or other pets.

Strangers are usually greeted with curiosity rather than aggression. Beardies are not typically guard dogs — they might bark to alert you to visitors, but they're more likely to wiggle up for a greeting than stand their ground. Early socialization is still important to prevent shyness, which can occasionally appear in the breed.

These dogs need mental stimulation as much as physical exercise. Without enough to do, they may become destructive or develop nuisance behaviors like excessive barking or chewing. Puzzle toys, training sessions, and dog sports help channel their considerable energy productively. Beardies thrive with owners who can match their enthusiasm and engage them consistently.

mikes_take.label: Mike's Take
mikes_take.heading: Mike's Honest Opinion on the Bearded Collie
mikes_take.html: The Beardie is genuinely one of the most fun dogs I've ever spent time around — they have this infectious, almost comedic energy that makes you smile even on a bad day. But they're absolutely not a breed for someone who wants a calm, low-maintenance companion; if you don't give a Beardie a job or serious daily exercise, you will regret it. For the right active family who loves grooming and doesn't mind a dog that's always 'on,' the Bearded Collie is pure magic.

care.label: Care
care.heading: Exercise, Training, and Daily Needs
care.html:
Bearded Collies require substantial daily exercise — at minimum 60 to 90 minutes of vigorous activity. This isn't a breed that will be satisfied with a short walk around the block. They excel at hiking, running, fetch, and dog sports. Off-leash exercise in a securely fenced area is ideal, as their herding instincts and energy can lead them to chase if allowed to roam freely.

Training should begin early and be consistent, positive, and varied. Beardies respond well to reward-based methods using treats, praise, and play. They do not respond well to harsh corrections and may become shut down or resistant if training is overly repetitive or punitive. Keeping sessions short, fun, and varied works best with this intelligent but independent breed.

Socialization is critical during the first year. Expose your Beardie puppy to as many different people, places, sounds, and animals as possible. Well-socialized Beardies are confident and adaptable; under-socialized ones may become nervous or overly reactive.

Grooming demands are significant (see the separate grooming guide for full detail). Daily or near-daily brushing is required to prevent the long coat from matting. Many pet owners opt to keep their Beardies in a shorter 'puppy cut' for easier maintenance, though this sacrifices the breed's signature look.

Beardies do best with access to a yard and need mental stimulation daily. Puzzle feeders, training games, and interactive play help meet their cognitive needs. They are not suited to apartment life unless their exercise needs are fully met through outdoor activities.

health.label: Health
health.heading: Common Health Concerns in Bearded Collies
health.html:
The Bearded Collie is generally a healthy breed with a lifespan of 12–14 years. However, like all breeds, they are predisposed to certain health conditions that prospective owners should be aware of.

Addison's Disease (Hypoadrenocorticism): The Bearded Collie has a notably elevated incidence of Addison's disease, an adrenal gland disorder affecting cortisol and aldosterone production. Symptoms include lethargy, weight loss, vomiting, and periodic crises. It is manageable with lifelong medication but can be life-threatening if undiagnosed.

Hypothyroidism: Underactive thyroid is relatively common in Beardies and can cause weight gain, lethargy, skin problems, and coat changes. It is diagnosed via bloodwork and treated with daily oral supplementation.

Hip Dysplasia: As with many medium and large breeds, hip dysplasia can occur. Reputable breeders screen breeding stock with OFA or PennHIP evaluations to reduce incidence in offspring.

Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA): This hereditary eye condition can affect Bearded Collies. Severity ranges from mild (no vision impact) to serious. DNA testing is available and should be performed on all breeding dogs.

Autoimmune Conditions: Beardies appear prone to certain autoimmune diseases beyond Addison's, including immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA) and autoimmune thyroiditis. Regular vet checkups and bloodwork help catch these conditions early.

To support your Beardie's health, choose a reputable breeder who screens for genetic health conditions, keep up with annual wellness exams, and maintain a healthy weight throughout the dog's life.

cost.label: Cost
cost.heading: What Does a Bearded Collie Cost?
cost.html:
Bearded Collies are not as widely bred as some herding dogs, which affects both availability and price. From a reputable breeder, expect to pay between $1,500 and $2,500 for a pet-quality Beardie puppy. Show-quality dogs from champion bloodlines may cost $3,000 or more. Adoption through a Beardie rescue organization typically runs $200–$500 and is a wonderful option for those open to adult dogs.

First-year ownership costs can be substantial. Budget for initial veterinary care including vaccinations, spay/neuter, and a baseline health panel — approximately $500–$1,000. Food for a medium-sized active dog runs $600–$900 per year for quality kibble or a fresh diet. Grooming supplies (professional-grade brush, detangling spray, slicker brush, comb) represent a one-time investment of $100–$200, plus ongoing professional grooming visits of $80–$150 per session if you opt for outside help.

Training classes, crates, bedding, toys, and puppy-proofing supplies add another $300–$600 in the first year. Pet insurance is strongly recommended given the breed's predisposition to Addison's disease — expect to pay $40–$80 per month for a comprehensive policy. Total first-year costs typically range from $3,500 to $5,500.

Ongoing annual costs after the first year average $2,000–$3,500, depending primarily on whether you groom at home or use a professional groomer, and whether any health issues arise.

right_for_you.label: Right for You?
right_for_you.heading: Is the Bearded Collie the Right Breed for Your Lifestyle?
good_fit: Have an active lifestyle with time for daily vigorous exercise
Enjoy grooming or are willing to invest in professional grooming
Want a dog that is deeply engaged with family life
Are interested in dog sports or activities
not_fit: You work full-time with 8+ hours away from home — Bearded Collies need 90+ min of vigorous daily activity, and under-exercised dogs of this breed often develop destructive chewing, barking, or separation anxiety
You can't commit 15-30 minutes daily to brushing or budget $80-150/month for professional grooming — Bearded Collie coats matt fast without consistent care
You work long hours and would leave the dog alone most of the day
You live in a small apartment without nearby outdoor space
You want a calm, easily managed dog
You have very young children and aren't prepared for a boisterous, energetic dog

finding.label: Finding a Bearded Collie
finding.heading: Finding a Reputable Bearded Collie Breeder or Rescue
finding.html:
The Bearded Collie Club of America (BCCA) is the AKC parent club for the breed and maintains a breeder referral list. This is one of the best starting points for finding a responsible breeder who health-tests their dogs and socializes puppies properly. Reputable breeders will welcome questions, allow you to meet the parents, and provide health clearances including OFA hip and elbow evaluations and DNA tests for CEA and Addison's-related markers.

Be cautious of breeders who always have puppies available, sell through third-party websites, or are unwilling to provide health documentation. Bearded Collies are not a high-volume breed, so wait lists with reputable breeders are common — plan ahead and be patient.

Rescue is a wonderful alternative. Beardie rescue organizations rehome dogs whose owners can no longer care for them, often providing thorough temperament assessments. Adult Beardies from rescue can be excellent companions, especially for experienced dog owners who want to skip the demanding puppy stage. Search for 'Bearded Collie rescue' along with your regional location to find groups near you.

faq.q: Do Bearded Collies shed a lot?
faq.a: Bearded Collies shed moderately year-round, with heavier shedding during seasonal coat blows. Their long coat can spread hair throughout the home, but regular brushing significantly reduces shedding. Many owners keep their Beardies in a shorter clip to manage shedding more easily.

faq.q: Are Bearded Collies good apartment dogs?
faq.a: Generally, Beardies are not ideal apartment dogs because of their high energy level and need for space to run. However, a very committed owner who provides 90+ minutes of vigorous daily outdoor exercise could make it work. A house with a fenced yard is strongly preferred.

faq.q: How much exercise does a Bearded Collie need daily?
faq.a: A healthy adult Bearded Collie needs at least 60–90 minutes of vigorous exercise every day. This should include active running, fetch, or off-leash play — not just leash walks. Mental stimulation through training and puzzle games is equally important.

faq.q: Are Bearded Collies easy to train?
faq.a: Beardies are intelligent and capable of learning quickly, but their independent nature means they require patient, consistent, and engaging training. They respond best to positive reinforcement and do not do well with repetitive drills or harsh corrections. Early training classes are strongly recommended.

faq.q: What is Addison's disease and why are Bearded Collies prone to it?
faq.a: Addison's disease is a failure of the adrenal glands to produce sufficient hormones. Bearded Collies have a genetic predisposition to the condition. Signs include lethargy, poor appetite, vomiting, and intermittent weakness. It's manageable with medication but can be fatal if not diagnosed. Regular vet visits and awareness of the signs are important for Beardie owners.
